sections.b: In the first round of the debate Job answers Bildad and Zophar (Job 9–10; Job 12–14). He turns the friends' question 'how can a mortal be in the right with God?' into a lawsuit: he cannot win a case against a God who is both his opponent and his judge, and he wishes for someone to 'stand between us to judge the case' (Job 9:33). He prays to God as the one whose hands formed him (Job 10:8–12), accuses the friends of 'lies on God's behalf' (Job 13:7), resolves to argue his case to God's face though it may cost his life (Job 13:15), and ends with a meditation on death: 'A tree, at least, has hope' (Job 14:7). For a moment he imagines God hiding him in Sheol and calling him back (Job 14:13–15), the first reach past death in the book.

common: 'Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him' (Job 13:15, KJV) is the best-known line of Job's faith.
uncommon: The written Hebrew of Job 13:15 says Job has nothing left to hope for; the famous 'I will hope in him' is the reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud.

sections.h: Bildad and Zophar on reward and punishment (Job 8; 11)
sections.b: Bildad states the doctrine at its plainest: 'Does God twist justice?' (Job 8:3). If Job's children died, they sinned; if Job is pure, God will restore him (Job 8:4–7). Zophar goes further: God is letting part of Job's guilt be forgotten (Job 11:6). Job answers with what he sees: 'wholehearted or wicked, he finishes them off' (Job 9:22), and robbers live in quiet tents (Job 12:6). The book lets both views speak at full strength before God's verdict that the friends did not speak rightly (Job 42:7), while Bildad's promise of a greater end still comes true (Job 8:7; Job 42:12).

common: Job's friends are often remembered as simply wrong, though most of what they say is found elsewhere in the Bible.

sections.b: From Job 9 the book speaks the language of the law court. Job asks how anyone can 'argue his case' with God (Job 9:3), complains that he could only beg 'the one who judges me' (Job 9:15), and wishes for someone to stand between them 'to judge the case' (Job 9:33). He asks God to state the charge (Job 10:2; Job 13:23), accuses the friends of 'lifting God's face', showing partiality in court (Job 13:8–10), sets his case in order (Job 13:18), and names the conditions of a fair hearing (Job 13:20–22). The lawsuit runs on to Job's signed oath in Job 31:35–37.

Job wishes: 'If only someone stood between us to judge the case, / to put his hand on each of us' (Job 9:33). The received Hebrew says flatly that there is no such umpire; the Greek, the Syriac and some Hebrew manuscripts make it a wish, and most modern commentators follow them. The Greek calls this figure a mesitēs, 'mediator', the word used of Christ in 1 Timothy 2:5. Job's longing grows into a witness in heaven who argues for a man with God (Job 16:19–21) and the redeemer of Job 19:25; Elihu speaks of an angel who intercedes (Job 33:23–24). Christians from Gregory the Great on heard Job's cry answered in Christ; Jewish readers have seen a longing for a heavenly advocate or a protest at an unequal trial.

uncommon: The received Hebrew of Job 9:33 says there is no umpire; the oldest translations, Hebrew idiom and most modern commentators make it a wish, 'if only there were'.

sections.h: The Sea and Rahab in Job 9
sections.b: Job praises the God who 'tramples on the back of the Sea' (Job 9:8), using the name Yam, the sea god of Canaanite myth, and says that 'Rahab's helpers crouched down under him' (Job 9:13), recalling the allies of the chaos monster in the old battle stories (compare the helpers of Tiamat in the Babylonian Enuma Elish). The Greek turns Rahab's helpers into 'the sea monsters under heaven'. Job returns to Rahab in Job 26:12, and God himself describes Leviathan in Job 41.
sections.refs: Job 7:12; Job 9:8; Job 9:13; Job 26:12–13; Psalm 89:10; Isaiah 51:9

sections.b: Job uses creation three ways. In Job 9:5–10 the Creator who moves mountains, commands the sun and made the Bear, Orion and the Pleiades is too great to face in court. In Job 10:8–12 God is the craftsman who shaped Job like clay, poured him like milk, set him like cheese and wove him with bones and sinews, one of the Bible's fullest pictures of a child forming in the womb, beside Psalm 139:13–16. In Job 12:7–10 the animals, the earth and the fish all know that 'the LORD's hand' made everything and holds every life.

Bildad finds wisdom in the tradition of the fathers (Job 8:8–10). Zophar says God's wisdom is 'higher than the heavens, deeper than Sheol' (Job 11:7–9), and that God would show Job its secrets (Job 11:6). Job mocks the friends' claim ('Wisdom will die when you do,' Job 12:2), questions whether age alone brings wisdom (Job 12:12), and claims all wisdom for God, though a wisdom that overturns kings and nations (Job 12:13–25). The question 'where can wisdom be found?' returns in Job 28.

Job calls Sheol 'the land of darkness and deep shadow', a place with 'no order' where even the light is gloom (Job 10:21–22). Zophar measures God's wisdom as 'deeper than Sheol' (Job 11:8). In Job 14 the dead lie down and do not wake 'until the heavens are gone' (Job 14:12); they do not know whether their sons are honored (Job 14:21). Yet Job dares to wish that God would hide him in Sheol until his anger passes and then remember him (Job 14:13), the first glimpse in the book of a hope beyond death.

common: Many readers assume the Old Testament teaches a clear afterlife of reward and punishment; Job 10 and 14 picture a shadowy Sheol for all.

sections.b: Job 10 and Job 13:20–14:22 are laments addressed to God, built from the language of the psalms: bitterness of soul (Job 10:1), the plea to be told the charge (Job 10:2), the appeal to God's past loyal love (Job 10:12), God's hidden face (Job 13:24; Psalm 13:1), and the frailty of human life (Job 14:1–2; Psalm 90; Psalm 103:15–16). Job stretches the form further than the psalms: he accuses God of a hidden plan (Job 10:13) and treats God as the enemy (Job 13:24), yet he never stops speaking to him.
sections.refs: Job 10:1–22; Job 13:20–28; Job 14:1–22; Psalm 13:1; Psalm 88; Psalm 90

sections.b: The best-known Ketiv and Qere in Job is in Job 13:15. The written letters have lo', 'not': Job has nothing left to hope for. The reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud has lo, 'for him': 'I will keep hoping in him' (KJV 'yet will I trust in him'). The two words sound the same; the variant on Job 13:15 gives the witnesses and the arguments. Other Ketiv/Qere pairs in these chapters are minor: 'snow' or 'snow water' (Job 9:30), 'let him stop' or 'stop!' (Job 10:20), and 'his limit' or 'his limits' (Job 14:5).

The speakers in Job's debate call God El, Eloah and Shaddai, 'the Almighty' (Job 8:3; Job 11:7), names that suit sages from outside Israel in the age of the ancestors. The personal name YHWH, 'the LORD', appears in the debate only once, in Job 12:9, a line that quotes Isaiah 41:20 ('the hand of the LORD has done this'). The narrator uses the name freely in the prologue, epilogue and the headings of the divine speeches.

Job's prayers are arguments. He asks God to state the charge (Job 10:2), reminds God of his own handiwork (Job 10:8–12), sets two conditions for a fair hearing (Job 13:20–21), and asks to be called or answered (Job 13:22). Zophar urges the traditional posture of repentance, palms spread to God (Job 11:13). Like Abraham (Genesis 18:25) and the lament psalms, Job treats prayer as a place where a person may contend with God, and God's verdict in Job 42:7 suggests this was not wrong.

Job says to God, 'You worked life and loyal love for me; / your watchful care guarded my breath' (Job 10:12). The memory of God's past hesed makes his present suffering harder to understand: the same God who formed him with care now seems to hunt him (Job 10:16). Job had also said that a man in despair should have loyal love from his friend (Job 6:14).

sections.h: God's hand over life and death (Job 12; 14)
sections.b: Job confesses that 'the LORD's hand' did everything and holds the life of every creature (Job 12:9–10), that God raises and destroys nations (Job 12:23), and that he has fixed the length of each human life, 'bounds he will not cross' (Job 14:5). For Job these truths are not yet a comfort: they mean that his suffering, too, is in God's hand.

sections.h: 'If he is not the one, then who is?' (Job 9:24)
sections.b: Job does not know of the Accuser's part in his suffering (Job 1–2), and he blames God directly: 'If he is not the one, then who is?' (Job 9:24). The Talmud records a debate over whether Job here spoke against God or only about the Accuser (Bava Batra 16a), and Rashi reads 'the wicked one' of Job 9:24 as the Accuser. The prologue itself does not let God off by blaming the Accuser: God says, 'you lured me against him' (Job 2:3).

sections.h: Bildad and Zophar in the first round (Job 8; 11)
sections.b: Bildad the Shuhite rests his case on tradition: 'Just ask the generation of long ago' (Job 8:8), for one short life cannot learn the truth alone (Job 8:9). His principle is that God does not twist justice (Job 8:3), so Job's children must have sinned and Job, if pure, will be restored (Job 8:4–7). Zophar the Naamathite rests on God's hidden wisdom, 'higher than the heavens, deeper than Sheol' (Job 11:7–8), and goes furthest of the three: God is letting part of Job's guilt be forgotten (Job 11:6). Both end with the fate of the wicked as a warning (Job 8:22; Job 11:20). With Eliphaz's vision (Job 4:12–21), the friends offer three kinds of certainty, and Job answers each (Job 12:3; Job 13:1–12).
